theme: Bildad speaks; Job questions God’s justice
readingInstruction: Read Job 8:1-10:22. Bildad speaks in chapter 8, and Job responds in chapters 9 and 10. Pay attention to the question Job asks in 9:2, because the whole book is about it.
settingTheScene: Bildad is the second friend to speak. Eliphaz relied on a personal experience. Bildad relies on tradition: what “the fathers” have taught. His speech is harder than Eliphaz’s. He even suggests that Job’s children died because of their own sin. Job answers with something new. He does not argue that he is innocent, but he asks a deeper question: even if a man were innocent, how could he ever win a case against God? He wishes there were someone to stand between them.
observation: Bildad asks, “Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert the right?” (8:3).
He says, “If your children have sinned against him, he has delivered them into the hand of their transgression” (8:4).
He tells Job that if he is pure and upright, God will rouse himself and restore him (8:5-6).
He appeals to the wisdom of earlier generations (8:8-10).
Job answers, “But how can a man be in the right before God?” (9:2).
He says that God is so powerful that no one can contend with him: “If it is a contest of strength, behold him! If it is a matter of justice, who can summon him?” (9:19).
Job says, “There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both” (9:33).
In chapter 10 he addresses God directly: “I loathe my life…I will say to God, Do not condemn me; let me know why you contend against me” (10:1-2).
He asks God, “Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese?” and remembers that God made him (10:10).
interpretation:
Bildad’s mistake is cruel, though he does not mean it to be. He does what the friends all do: he turns suffering into a verdict. The death of Job’s children is, to Bildad, proof that they were guilty. It is hard to imagine a colder thing to say to a grieving father. But notice that Bildad believes he is defending God. His first question is a real one: “Does God pervert justice?” The answer is no, and Job would agree. The error is in thinking that he understands how God’s justice works in every case.

Job’s answer is much deeper. The question in 9:2 is the central one: “How can a man be in the right before God?” Job is not asking about his own sin. He is asking something bigger. God is so great and so strong that no human being could stand before him in court. Even if I were innocent, he says, my own mouth would condemn me. He sees clearly what Bildad does not: that the real problem between God and humanity is not a technical question about who deserves what. It is the distance between a holy God and a creature.

That leads Job to the most important wish in the chapter. “There is no arbiter between us.” He wishes for a mediator, someone with a hand on God and a hand on Job, who could bring them together. Job does not yet know that he is longing for a person God will one day send. He only knows that he needs one.

In chapter 10 his wild words turn into something like faith. He remembers that God made him, shaped him like clay, and knit him together with bones and sinews (10:8-12). The one who is attacking him is the one who made him. That memory does not remove the pain, but it makes the pain a question rather than a verdict: if you made me, why are you doing this?

This is one of the strange gifts of Job. He is allowed to ask the question without being told that the question is out of bounds.
connection: Paul says that “there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). Hebrews 9:15 says Christ is “the mediator of a new covenant.” Job’s cry for an arbiter finds its answer in Jesus, who has laid a hand on God and on us. The picture of God as potter is also in Isaiah 64:8 and Romans 9:20-21.
application:
Do not think that you can win an argument with God. Ask instead for the Mediator. Spend time thanking Jesus for being the one who stands between you and the Father.

Also, notice how easy it is to comfort yourself by finding a reason that other people suffer, such as “they must have done something.” Resist that. Every time you catch yourself doing it, pray for the person instead.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what makes you feel unable to stand before him.
Thank Jesus for being the mediator Job longed for.
Ask him to make you gentle with those who suffer.
